The Damiano Defence (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6) is named after 16th-century chess author Pedro Damiano even though, in his own 1512 book, Damiano explicitly condemned 2...f6 as an inferior move that lets White gain the advantage with 3.Nxe5.

The Blackmar-Diemer Gambit is named for two people decades apart: 19th-century New Orleans player Armand Blackmar, who first published analysis of 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.f3, and 20th-century German master Emil Josef Diemer, who developed the sounder 3.Nc3-based version and promoted it in his 1950s book.

The Réti Opening is named after Richard Réti following his game against Akiba Rubinstein at Karlovy Vary 1923 (so dubbed by commentator Hans Kmoch); Réti's most famous use of it came in 1924 when he defeated World Champion José Raúl Capablanca in New York, ending Capablanca's eight-year unbeaten streak.

The joke opening 1.e4 e5 2.Ke2, known as the 'Bongcloud Attack,' was played by world champion Magnus Carlsen against Hikaru Nakamura in the 2021 Magnus Carlsen Invitational; Nakamura mirrored it with 2...Ke7, and the resulting 'Double Bongcloud' game was drawn by repeated king shuffling.

The oldest recorded game featuring the King's Gambit dates to 1560, played between Ruy López de Segura and Giovanni Leonardo Da Cutri, though the opening had already appeared in Luis Ramírez de Lucena's 1497 chess book.
trivia.source: chessjournal.com, '10 Oldest Chess Openings in History'

trivia.fact: The Queen's Gambit is not technically a true gambit, since White can almost always recapture the offered c-pawn (typically via e3 and Bxc4) without any lasting material sacrifice, unlike a genuine gambit where the pawn is permanently risked.
The Queen's Gambit was also historically called the 'Aleppo Gambit' after the 18th-century Syrian-born chess theorist Philipp Stamma of Aleppo, who recommended the opening.

The Colle System is named after Belgian master Edgard Colle, who introduced and played 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 from 1925 until his death in 1932 at age 34, following complications from a fourth operation for a gastric ulcer.

The Trompowsky Attack (1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5) is named after Brazilian champion Octávio Trompowsky, who played it in the 1930s and 1940s; it is also known as the Opočenský Opening after Czech master Karel Opočenský, who used it in the same era.

The Latvian Gambit was originally called the Greco Counter-Gambit after 17th-century Italian player Gioachino Greco; FIDE officially renamed it the Latvian Gambit at its 1937 Congress in tribute to Latvian analyst Kārlis Bētiņš, who had deeply studied the line.

The Pirc Defence is named after Slovenian grandmaster Vasja Pirc, who played it from the late 1940s onward; in Russia and other former Soviet countries it is often called the Ufimtsev Defence (or Pirc–Ufimtsev), after Soviet master Anatoly Ufimtsev.

A possible early ancestor of the Scandinavian Defence appears in the Catalan poem 'Scachs d'amor' (c. 1475), a fictional game set in Valencia between Francesc de Castellví and Narcís Vinyoles, believed to be among the earliest documented games using the modern queen and bishop moves.
The Vienna Game owes its name to 19th-century Viennese analysts; Austrian master Carl Hamppe contributed so heavily to its theory that the opening was for a time known as the 'Hamppe Opening'.
trivia.source: chessklub.com, 'The Vienna Game - A Scholarly Guide'

trivia.fact: The Zukertort Opening (1.Nf3) is named after Johannes Zukertort, who employed it from his 1880 match against Samuel Rosenthal onward, even though the move itself predates him and had already appeared in games by Howard Staunton, Adolf Anderssen, and Paul Morphy.

Miguel Najdorf first played the Sicilian move 5...a6 (now the Najdorf Variation) in 1939, but the line only broke through internationally at the 1947 Prague tournament, later becoming the signature weapon of Bobby Fischer, Garry Kasparov, and Viswanathan Anand.

The term 'Indian Defence' for openings like 1.d4 Nf6 was first used in 1884, but the specific modern names 'King's Indian Defence' and 'King's Indian Attack' are attributed to mid-20th-century chess writer Hans Kmoch.

The King's Indian Defence was considered highly suspect until the 1940s, when Soviet players David Bronstein, Isaac Boleslavsky, and Alexander Konstantinopolsky's analysis and results made it a respected, popular opening.

Owen's Defence (1.e4 b6) is named after English vicar John Owen, who in 1858 won one individual game against touring American master Paul Morphy in an odds match, despite starting that game with pawn-and-move odds and losing the overall match 6–1.

The Englund Gambit is named after Swedish player Fritz Englund not because he invented it, but because he sponsored a thematic tournament in Stockholm from late 1932 to early 1933 in which every game had to start from the position after 4.Qd5; the main line is actually credited to Kārlis Bētiņš.

Grob's Attack (1.g4) is named after Swiss International Master Henri Grob, who wrote a 1942 book on it titled 'Angriff g2-g4'; Grob himself called it the 'Spike Opening,' and it was earlier known as 'Ahlhausen's Opening' after 19th-century Berlin player Carl Ahlhausen.

Both Fool's Mate and Scholar's Mate were named and described in Francis Beale's 1656 book 'The Royall Game of Chesse-Play,' which adapted the earlier work of 17th-century Italian player Gioachino Greco.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Fool's mate; Wikipedia: Scholar's mate

trivia.fact: 'Scholar's mate' originally meant 'student's mate' — in 17th-century English, 'scholler' referred to a pupil or beginner rather than an expert, reflecting that the four-move trap is typically sprung by and against inexperienced players.

The 'Immortal Game' between Adolf Anderssen and Lionel Kieseritzky was played as an informal (non-tournament) game in London on June 21, 1851, during a break in the first international chess tournament.
In the Immortal Game, Anderssen sacrificed a bishop, both rooks, and his queen, then delivered checkmate using only his knight, bishop, and a pawn, while Kieseritzky had lost just three pawns.
The Immortal Game was given its name in 1855 by the Austrian problemist and chess writer Ernst Falkbeer.
The 'Evergreen Game' was a casual Evans Gambit played by Adolf Anderssen against Jean Dufresne in Berlin in 1852.
In the Evergreen Game, Anderssen sacrificed his queen with 21.Qxd7+, forcing a mating sequence with his bishops a few moves later.
The Evergreen Game was named by Wilhelm Steinitz, who called it 'an evergreen in the laurel crown' of Anderssen.

The 'Opera Game' was a consultation game played by Paul Morphy (White, alone) against Duke Karl of Brunswick and Count Isouard (jointly playing Black) at the Salle Le Peletier opera house in Paris in 1858.
Morphy won the Opera Game in just 17 moves, finishing with a queen sacrifice and checkmate delivered by his rooks and bishop.

The 'Game of the Century' was played between Donald Byrne (White) and 13-year-old Bobby Fischer (Black) at the Rosenwald Memorial tournament at the Marshall Chess Club in New York City on October 17, 1956.
trivia.source: chessgames.com gid=1008361; Wikipedia 'Game of the Century (chess)'

trivia.fact: In the Game of the Century, Fischer sacrificed his queen with 17...Be6!!, receiving a rook, two bishops, and a pawn in return, and went on to win.
trivia.source: chessgames.com gid=1008361; Wikipedia 'Game of the Century (chess)'

trivia.fact: The name 'Game of the Century' was coined by chess journalist Hans Kmoch, writing in Chess Review.
'Kasparov's Immortal' is Garry Kasparov's win as White over Veselin Topalov at the Hoogovens tournament in Wijk aan Zee in 1999, launched by the piece sacrifice 24.Rxd4!!.

In Kasparov's Immortal vs. Topalov, Kasparov's combination included three separate rook sacrifices as he chased Topalov's king across the board before finishing with the decisive bishop retreat 36.Bf1.
trivia.source: Chess.com 'The Greatest Chess Game Of All Time Explained'; chessgames.com gid=1011478

trivia.fact: Chess.com's editorial ranking of the greatest chess games ever played lists Kasparov vs. Topalov, Wijk aan Zee 1999, at number one.
trivia.source: Chess.com 'The Greatest Chess Game Of All Time Explained — Kasparov vs. Topalov, 1999'

trivia.fact: In Game 6 of the 1997 rematch, played in New York on May 11, 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov in a Caro-Kann Steinitz Variation, with the computer playing the sharp knight sacrifice 8.Nxe6.

Kasparov resigned Game 6 of the 1997 Deep Blue rematch after just 19 moves, clinching the match for Deep Blue at 3.5-2.5 — the first time a computer had beaten a reigning World Chess Champion in a multi-game match under standard time controls.
trivia.source: Wikipedia 'Deep Blue versus Kasparov, 1997, Game 6'; History.com 'Deep Blue defeats Garry Kasparov in chess match'

trivia.fact: Game 2 of the 1997 Deep Blue–Kasparov rematch became notorious after Kasparov resigned in a position that later computer analysis suggested was defensible or drawn; he initially suspected IBM of receiving covert human grandmaster help, a claim he significantly walked back in a 2016 interview.
trivia.source: Chess.com 'Garry Kasparov: Success, Deep Blue, After 1997 And The Controversy'; Wikipedia 'Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov'

trivia.fact: On February 10, 1996, in Philadelphia, Deep Blue beat Kasparov in Game 1 of their first match (a Sicilian, Alapin Variation), the first win by a chess computer over a reigning World Champion under normal tournament time controls.
Despite losing Game 1 in 1996, Kasparov won the overall six-game match against Deep Blue 4-2, winning three games and drawing two of the remainder.
Kasparov won Game 1 of the 1997 Deep Blue rematch, played May 3, 1997 in New York, in 45 moves.
trivia.source: Chess.com 'Kasparov vs. Deep Blue (1997)'; chessgames.com gid=1070917

trivia.fact: The 'Gold Coins Game' was won by Frank Marshall against Stepan Levitsky in Breslau (now Wrocław) on July 20, 1912, during the DSB Congress masters' tournament.
Marshall's winning move against Levitsky, 23...Qg3!!, placed his queen en prise to three different white pieces simultaneously, with no adequate defense; Levitsky resigned immediately.

According to Marshall's own 1942 memoir 'My Fifty Years of Chess,' spectators showered the board with gold coins after his 23...Qg3!! move — though this account has been disputed by other witnesses, including Marshall's wife.
trivia.source: Wikipedia 'Levitsky versus Marshall'; chesshistory.com 'Marshall's Gold Coins Game' by Edward Winter

trivia.fact: In round 10 of Hastings 1895 (played August 17), Wilhelm Steinitz defeated Curt von Bardeleben in a game that became known as 'The Battle of Hastings.'
trivia.source: chessgames.com gid=1132699; chesshistory.com 'Steinitz v von Bardeleben' by Edward Winter

trivia.fact: Facing a demonstrated forced mate in ten moves against him, Curt von Bardeleben simply got up and walked out of the tournament hall rather than resign, letting his clock run out instead.
trivia.source: chesshistory.com 'Steinitz v von Bardeleben' by Edward Winter; Wikipedia 'Curt von Bardeleben'

trivia.fact: 'Rubinstein's Immortal' was played between Georg Rotlewi and Akiba Rubinstein in Łódź on December 26, 1907, a Tarrasch Defense in which Rubinstein sacrificed his queen and a rook to force checkmate.
The name 'Rubinstein's Immortal' for the Rotlewi game was coined by chess writer Hans Kmoch, and Garry Kasparov later called it Rubinstein's 'most famous creation.'

The 'Polish Immortal' is a game won by the 19-year-old Miguel Najdorf as Black against a player named Glucksberg in Warsaw (most commonly dated 1929, though some sources give 1930 or 1935), in which Najdorf sacrificed all four of his minor pieces in a mating attack.
In the Polish Immortal, Najdorf delivered checkmate in 22 moves after his sequence of four consecutive minor-piece sacrifices.
At Tilburg on October 21, 1991, Nigel Short marched his own castled king up the board with 31.Kh2, 32.Kg3, 33.Kh4, and 34.Kg5 against Jan Timman, who resigned rather than face the mating threat.
The Short–Timman 'king walk' game was voted one of the 100 greatest chess games of all time by authors Graham Burgess, John Nunn, and John Emms.
trivia.source: Chess.com 'Short's Immortal King Walk — Every Chess Move Explained'

trivia.fact: In Game 6 of the 1972 World Championship in Reykjavik, Bobby Fischer played the Queen's Gambit for the first time in a serious tournament game against Boris Spassky, and won.
After losing Game 6 of the 1972 World Championship, Spassky stood up and joined the roughly 1,500 spectators in Reykjavik in applauding Fischer's performance.

Game 13 of the 1972 World Championship (Fischer as Black, Alekhine's Defense) was adjourned at move 42 and resumed the next day; Fischer won a complex rook-versus-pawns endgame after Spassky erred around move 69.
trivia.source: Chess.com '50 year anniversary Fischer-Spassky Game 13'; chessgames.com gid=1128889

trivia.fact: Former World Champion Mikhail Botvinnik called Fischer's Game 13 win over Spassky in 1972 'the highest creative achievement of Fischer.'

'Kasparov versus the World' was an internet consultation game hosted by the MSN Gaming Zone in 1999, in which a 'World Team' of thousands of players voted on each move for Black against Garry Kasparov, who played White alone.

The Kasparov versus the World game lasted 62 moves over roughly four months (June-October 1999); the World Team resigned after Kasparov's 62.g7, and Kasparov called it 'the greatest game in the history of chess.'
In Game 16 of the 1985 World Championship in Moscow, Garry Kasparov planted a knight on d3 with 16...Nd3, an outpost that paralyzed Anatoly Karpov's position for many moves.
trivia.source: Chess.com 'World Chess Championship 1985: Game 16'; chessgames.com gid=1067175

trivia.fact: Karpov was finally forced to give up his queen to remove Kasparov's d3 knight with 34.Qxd3, after which 34...Nf2+ forked king and queen and Kasparov went on to win.
Kasparov won the 1985 World Championship match against Karpov 13-11, becoming the youngest World Chess Champion in history at age 22 (a record he still held as of this writing).
Bobby Fischer's win over Robert Byrne in the 1963/64 U.S. Championship in New York was awarded the tournament's brilliancy prize, featuring the shocking sacrifice 18...Nxg2!!.
trivia.source: chessgames.com gid=1008419; Chess.com 'Bobby Fischer's Perfect US Championship Game'

trivia.fact: Fischer won the 1963/64 U.S. Championship with a perfect score of 11 wins and 0 losses/draws, and included his brilliancy-prize win over Robert Byrne in his book 'My 60 Memorable Games.'

Rashid Nezhmetdinov's queen sacrifice 12.Qxf6!! against Oleg Chernikov, played in Rostov-on-Don in the 1962 Chigorin Team Cup, is frequently cited as one of the greatest queen sacrifices in chess history.
trivia.source: chessgames.com gid=1260278; Chess.com 'Nezhmetdinov's Immortal Queen Sacrifice'

trivia.fact: The 'Immortal Zugzwang Game' was won by Aron Nimzowitsch against Friedrich Sämisch in round 6 of a tournament in Copenhagen in March 1923, with the final position (after 25...h6) long described as a rare middlegame zugzwang.

In September 2002, playing a rapid game (25 minutes plus 10-second increment) in the Russia vs. Rest of the World match in Moscow, Judit Polgar defeated Garry Kasparov, the world's top-ranked player — the first time a woman had beaten the world number one in a competitive game.

Frank Marshall unveiled his prepared pawn-sacrifice novelty, later named the Marshall Attack, against José Raúl Capablanca in the first round of the Manhattan Chess Club Masters tournament in New York on October 23, 1918; Capablanca found the defense over the board and won.

On November 22, 1938, in round 11 of the AVRO tournament in Rotterdam, Mikhail Botvinnik defeated José Raúl Capablanca in a Nimzo-Indian with two piece sacrifices; Garry Kasparov later called it the 'game of his life' for Botvinnik.
trivia.source: chessgames.com gid=1031957; Wikipedia 'Botvinnik versus Capablanca, AVRO 1938'

trivia.fact: At Linares 1998, Alexei Shirov (Black) played the bishop sacrifice 47...Bh3!! against Veselin Topalov in an opposite-colored-bishop endgame, a move ranked number one in John Emms' book 'The Most Amazing Chess Moves of All Time.'
trivia.source: chessgames.com gid=1143956; Chess.com 'Brilliant Endgames, Shirov Style'

trivia.fact: Alexander Alekhine called his 1925 win over Richard Réti at Baden-Baden the finest game of his career, and noted that ironically neither it nor his 1922 Hastings win over Efim Bogoljubov received a brilliancy prize, since none was on offer at either event.
trivia.source: chesshistory.com 'Réti v Alekhine, Baden-Baden, 1925' by Edward Winter

trivia.fact: In Game 6 of the 1960 World Championship match in Moscow, Mikhail Tal sacrificed a knight against Mikhail Botvinnik with 21...Nf4!! in a King's Indian Defense; Tal went on to win the match by four points, becoming the youngest World Chess Champion up to that time at age 23.
trivia.source: Chess.com 'Mikhail Tal's Greatest Game! — Botvinnik vs. Tal, 1960'; Wikipedia 'World Chess Championship 1960'

trivia.fact: The youngest person ever to earn the Grandmaster title is Abhimanyu Mishra of the United States, who qualified at age 12 years, 4 months, and 25 days in 2021, breaking Sergey Karjakin's 19-year-old record.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Abhimanyu Mishra; Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Argentina's Faustino Oro became the second-youngest grandmaster in history at 12 years, 6 months, and 26 days, earning his final GM norm at the Sardinia World Chess Festival in Orosei, Italy on May 10, 2026.
trivia.source: Chess.com news: 'Faustino Oro' GM norm coverage, May 2026; WorldChess.com

trivia.fact: Before Mishra, Sergey Karjakin held the youngest-grandmaster record for 19 years after qualifying in 2002 at age 12 years, 7 months.
Judit Polgar broke Bobby Fischer's 33-year-old youngest-grandmaster record in December 1991, qualifying at 15 years, 4 months, becoming the first woman ever to hold the record.
Bobby Fischer became a grandmaster at age 15 years, 6 months, 1 day in 1958 (via the Portorož Interzonal), the youngest grandmaster in the world at the time.
Hikaru Nakamura became the youngest American to earn the grandmaster title, at 15 years and 79 days in 2003, breaking Bobby Fischer's US record by about three months.
The highest FIDE classical chess rating ever officially attained is 2882, achieved by Magnus Carlsen (Norway) in May 2014 and matched again in August 2019 — still the record as of 2026.
trivia.source: Guinness World Records: 'Highest Chess Rating, Men'

trivia.fact: Magnus Carlsen's highest unofficial live FIDE rating was 2889.2, reached on April 21, 2014, ahead of that month's official list publication.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess; ChessWorld.net

trivia.fact: The highest FIDE rating ever achieved by a woman is 2735, by Judit Polgar in July 2005 — a record that still stands as of 2026, more than two decades later.
trivia.source: Guinness World Records: 'Highest Chess Rating, Women'

trivia.fact: Judit Polgar is the only woman to have ever broken a 2700 FIDE rating, and she was the world's top-rated woman continuously from January 1989 until her retirement in 2014 — a 26-year streak.
trivia.source: Chess.com; Yahoo Sports interview with Judit Polgár

trivia.fact: Bobby Fischer holds the record for the largest rating lead over the world's #2 player: 125 Elo points, in July 1972 after winning the world championship.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Garry Kasparov spent a cumulative 255 months (roughly 21 years) ranked world No. 1 on the FIDE rating list, the longest of any player in history.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Alireza Firouzja is the youngest player ever to surpass a 2800 FIDE rating, doing so at 18 years and 166 days old in December 2021, breaking Magnus Carlsen's previous record of 18 years, 336 days.
trivia.source: FIDE (via X/Twitter); Chess.com news: 'Alireza Firouzja Youngest Chess Player Ever To Break 2800'

trivia.fact: The longest decisive FIDE-rated tournament game on record is Billy Fellowes vs. Peter Lalić, played at the Third Kingston Invitational in London in 2024, lasting 272 moves.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: The longest tournament chess game overall (by move count) is Ivan Nikolić vs. Goran Arsović, Belgrade 1989 (Yugoslav Championship), which ran 269 moves over 20 hours 15 minutes before ending in a draw.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess; Chess.com

trivia.fact: The longest game ever played in a World Chess Championship match is Game 6 of Carlsen vs. Nepomniachtchi at the 2021 World Chess Championship: 136 moves, won by Carlsen after nearly 8 hours, ending a streak of 19 consecutive drawn classical WCC games going back 5 years.
trivia.source: Chess.com news: 'Carlsen Wins Game 6, Longest World Chess Championship Game Of All Time'; ESPN

trivia.fact: Before 2021, the longest World Championship game was Game 5 of Korchnoi vs. Karpov in Baguio City, 1978, at 124 moves — it ended in a stalemate.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: The fewest possible moves to deliver checkmate is two, known as Fool's Mate (e.g., 1.g4 e5 2.f3 Qh4#).
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: The shortest decisive game between titled masters on record is Đorđević–Kovačević, Bela Crkva 1984, decided in just 3 moves (1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 c6 3.e3?? Qa5+ winning the bishop).
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: The shortest tournament loss by a grandmaster is 4 moves — GM Yair Kraidman lost to IM Hagen Poetsch at the 2013 Vienna Open after miscalculating a queen recapture.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: D Gukesh of India became the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion in history in December 2024, at 18 years, 6 months, 14 days old, defeating Ding Liren 7.5–6.5 — breaking Garry Kasparov's 39-year-old record (set in 1985 at age 22).
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess; ChessBase: '35 years ago: Kasparov becomes youngest World Champion'

trivia.fact: Ruslan Ponomariov was the youngest FIDE (knockout-format) World Champion, winning the title in January 2002 at age 18 years, 3 months, 13 days.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Hou Yifan became the youngest Women's World Chess Champion in history in 2010, at 16 years, 9 months, 27 days old.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Vera Menchik was the first and longest-reigning Women's World Chess Champion, holding the title for 17 years (1927–1944) and winning all eight championship tournaments she entered.
trivia.source: FIDE (via X/Twitter, official account); Wikipedia: Vera Menchik

trivia.fact: Vera Menchik won at least 59 consecutive games at the Women's World Championship tournaments, going undefeated across four straight events (1931–1937) with a combined score of 45 wins, 0 losses, 0 draws in those events.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess; Wikipedia: Vera Menchik

trivia.fact: Nona Gaprindashvili reigned as Women's World Champion for 16 years (1962–1978) and in 1978 became the first woman ever awarded the FIDE Grandmaster title.
Emanuel Lasker holds the record for the longest reign of any officially recognized World Chess Champion: 27 years, from 1894 (defeating Steinitz) until his loss to Capablanca in 1921.
trivia.source: Chess.com: '27 Years as World Champion!'; Wikipedia: Emanuel Lasker

trivia.fact: José Raúl Capablanca went undefeated in serious competition for over 8 years — from a loss to Oscar Chajes on February 10, 1916, until a loss to Richard Réti on March 21, 1924 — a streak of 63 games (40 wins, 23 draws) spanning his 1921 World Championship win.
Wilhelm Steinitz holds the longest documented winning streak in chess history: 25 consecutive game wins spread across nine years, from Vienna 1873 to Vienna 1882.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Magnus Carlsen holds the modern elite-level record for longest unbeaten streak in classical chess: 125 games (42 wins, 83 draws, zero losses) from July 31, 2018 to October 9, 2020, ended by Jan-Krzysztof Duda at Norway Chess. His opponents during the streak averaged a 2745 rating.
trivia.source: Guinness World Records: 'Longest unbeaten streak in professional chess'; CNN

trivia.fact: Before Carlsen, the elite-level unbeaten-streak record was held by Sergei Tiviakov at 110 games (2004–2005), and before that by Ding Liren at 100 games.
trivia.source: Guinness World Records: 'Longest unbeaten streak in professional chess'

trivia.fact: Bobby Fischer won 20 consecutive games against world-class competition in the 1970–71 World Championship cycle: closing the Palma de Mallorca Interzonal with 7 straight wins, then sweeping the Candidates matches 6–0 over Mark Taimanov, 6–0 over Bent Larsen, and winning the first game against Tigran Petrosian.
trivia.source: Chess.com; multiple sources on Fischer's 1970-71 Candidates run

trivia.fact: Tigran Petrosian holds the record for most Chess Olympiad medals by an individual: 9 gold and 1 silver across 10 Olympiads (1958–1978) for the USSR, losing just a single game in his entire Olympiad career.

The 1984–85 Karpov vs. Kasparov World Championship match is the longest in history: it ran 5 months (September 10, 1984 to February 15, 1985) and 48 games before being controversially terminated without a result by FIDE President Florencio Campomanes, with Karpov leading 5–3 (40 draws).
Before the 1984–85 match, the longest World Championship match was Capablanca vs. Alekhine in 1927, at 34 games.

The 2018 World Chess Championship between Magnus Carlsen and Fabiano Caruana is the only one in history where all 12 classical games ended in draws; Carlsen then won the rapid tiebreak 3–0. This broke the previous record of 8 consecutive WCC draws set by Anand vs. Kasparov in 1995.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: World Chess Championship 2018; Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Garry Kasparov's 1997 loss to IBM's Deep Blue (3.5–2.5 in the rematch) was the first defeat of a reigning World Chess Champion by a computer under tournament match conditions; Kasparov had won the 1996 match 4–2.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov; History.com

trivia.fact: Ehsan Ghaem-Maghami of Iran set the Guinness World Record for most simultaneous chess games played by an individual: 604 opponents over 25 hours at Shahid Beheshti University, Tehran, February 8–9, 2011, winning 580 games for a 97.35% score.
trivia.source: Guinness World Records: 'Most simultaneous games of chess by an individual'; Wikipedia: Ehsan Ghaem Maghami

trivia.fact: The most games of chess ever played simultaneously in one location is 20,480, set by the Sports Authority of Gujarat in Ahmedabad, India, on December 24, 2010, with World Champion Viswanathan Anand making the ceremonial opening moves.
trivia.source: Guinness World Records: 'Most games of chess played simultaneously in one location'

trivia.fact: American grandmaster Timur Gareyev holds the blindfold simultaneous chess record: 48 opponents at once over roughly 20 hours at UNLV in December 2016, scoring 35 wins, 7 draws, 6 losses (while riding an exercise bike throughout).
trivia.source: Chess.com news: 'Timur Gareyev Plays Record 48 Games Blindfolded - Now Recognized By Guinness'

trivia.fact: José Raúl Capablanca's best simultaneous exhibition result was 102 wins and 1 draw against 103 opponents in Cleveland in 1922, a 99.5% score in seven hours.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: The Guinness World Record for longest chess marathon is 64 hours, set by Tunde Onakoya (Nigeria) and Shawn Martinez (USA) in Times Square, New York City, April 17–20, 2025, comprising 473 games — breaking the prior record of 61 hours 3 minutes 34 seconds set at 2024 Norway Chess.
trivia.source: Guinness World Records: 'Longest chess marathon'; Chess.com news

trivia.fact: The longest correspondence chess game by real-world duration is a single game between Dr. Reinhart Straszacker and Dr. Hendrik van Huyssteen that lasted over 53 years, begun in 1946 and ended only by Straszacker's death in 1999 (part of a 112-game series they split evenly).
trivia.source: Guinness World Records: 'Longest duration playing correspondence chess'

trivia.fact: Judit Polgar defeated then-world-#1 Garry Kasparov in a classical game in September 2002 — Kasparov was rated 2838 to her 2681, a 157-point rating upset, considered one of the biggest shocks against a reigning top player.
trivia.source: TheChessWorld: '10 Epic Upsets in Chess History'

trivia.fact: Bobby Fischer became the youngest-ever U.S. Chess Champion at age 14 when he won the 1957–58 U.S. Championship, a record that stood for decades.
Hikaru Nakamura became the youngest U.S. Chess Champion since Bobby Fischer when he won the 2005 U.S. Championship at age 17.
Yuri Averbakh became the first-ever centenarian chess grandmaster, turning 100 on February 8, 2022; he remains the only grandmaster known to have lived to age 100.
trivia.source: FIDE: 'The oldest living Grandmaster Yuri Averbakh turns 100'

trivia.fact: American IM Anthony Saidy set the record for oldest player to defeat a grandmaster, beating GM Vladimir Belous at the 2019 National Open at age 82 years, 1 month.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: India's Ashwath Kaushik set the record for youngest player ever to defeat a grandmaster, beating GM Jacek Stopa on February 18, 2024, at age 8 years, 6 months, 11 days.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Fabiano Caruana posted a 3098 performance rating at the 2014 Sinquefield Cup — among the highest performance ratings ever recorded in a top-level round-robin against elite competition, going 7/10 including a 7-win start.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: List of world records in chess

trivia.fact: Viktor Korchnoi was still competing at grandmaster level into his 80s, reported as the oldest grandmaster on the active world tournament circuit around 2012 (he died in 2016 at age 85).
Alan Turing and David Champernowne devised 'Turochamp' in 1948, a chess-playing algorithm executed by hand (a 'paper machine') since no computer of the day could run it.
In 1952, Alan Turing personally executed the Turochamp algorithm by hand move-by-move in a game against colleague Alick Glennie, and lost in 29 moves.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Turochamp; Chess.com 'The History Of Computer Chess: Turochamp'

trivia.fact: Claude Shannon's 1950 paper 'Programming a Computer for Playing Chess' (Philosophical Magazine, Vol. 41, No. 314) laid the theoretical foundation for computer chess, including minimax search with an evaluation function.
trivia.source: Chessprogramming wiki: Claude Shannon; Philosophical Magazine Vol 41 No 314

trivia.fact: Shannon's 1950 paper classified chess programs into 'Type A' (brute-force search of all moves to a uniform depth) and 'Type B' (selective search of only plausible moves) strategies.
trivia.source: Chessprogramming wiki: Type B Strategy / Brute-Force

trivia.fact: The first chess-like game played by a computer was on the MANIAC I at Los Alamos in 1956, written by Stanislaw Ulam, Paul Stein, Mark Wells, James Kister, William Walden and John Pasta, using a reduced 6x6 board without bishops (later called Los Alamos Chess) because the machine lacked power for full chess.
trivia.source: Chessprogramming wiki: MANIAC I; Wikipedia: Los Alamos chess

trivia.fact: The MANIAC I program searched only 4 plies deep, taking about 12 minutes per move at roughly 11,000 operations/second, and in its third game defeated a novice human player -- the first recorded computer win against a person in a chess-like game.

The first-ever match between two chess computer programs was the Kotok-McCarthy program (Stanford, on an IBM 7090) versus the ITEP program (Moscow, on an M-20), a four-game correspondence match begun November 22, 1966 and finished in 1967, won 3-1 by the Soviet ITEP program.

The First World Computer Chess Championship was held August 5-8, 1974 in Stockholm, Sweden, organized under IFIP with 13 participating programs; the Soviet program Kaissa won with a perfect 4/4 score.

In 1983, Ken Thompson (software) and Joe Condon (hardware)'s chess computer Belle became the first computer to earn a USCF Master rating, after scoring a 2363 performance rating in the U.S. Open; it won the $5,000 Fredkin Prize as the first program to reach master strength.
trivia.source: IEEE Spectrum: 'In 1983, This Bell Labs Computer Was the First Machine to Become a Chess Master'; Wikipedia: Belle (chess machine)

trivia.fact: In 1988, Deep Thought -- built by Feng-hsiung Hsu, Murray Campbell, Thomas Anantharaman and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon -- became the first computer to defeat a grandmaster (Bent Larsen) in a regular tournament game, at the Software Toolworks Open in Long Beach, California.

Deep Thought was named after the fictional supercomputer in Douglas Adams' 'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy'; after its 1989 two-game loss to Garry Kasparov, IBM held a naming contest and the machine was rechristened 'Deep Blue' -- a play on 'Deep Thought' and IBM's corporate nickname 'Big Blue' -- with the winning name submitted by Peter Fitzhugh Brown.

Key members of the Deep Thought team (Feng-hsiung Hsu and Murray Campbell) moved from Carnegie Mellon to IBM's T.J. Watson Research Center around 1989-1990, where Deep Thought's design evolved into Deep Blue.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Feng-hsiung Hsu; Wikipedia: Deep Thought (chess computer)

trivia.fact: Garry Kasparov won the first Deep Blue match, played in Philadelphia February 10-17, 1996, by a score of 4-2 (one loss, two draws, three wins for Kasparov); Deep Blue's Game 1 win was the first game won by a chess computer against a reigning world champion under normal time controls.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov; History.com

trivia.fact: In the May 1997 rematch in New York, Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov 3.5-2.5, becoming the first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion in a full match under standard tournament time controls; Kasparov resigned the decisive Game 6 after just 19 moves on May 11, 1997.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov; History.com: 'Deep Blue defeats Garry Kasparov in chess match'

trivia.fact: Deep Blue was an IBM RS/6000 SP supercomputer using 30 PowerPC 604e processors paired with 480 custom VLSI 'chess chips,' giving it a sustained match search speed of roughly 200 million chess positions per second.

After Deep Blue's Game 2 win in 1997, Kasparov accused IBM of cheating, citing an unusual move (37.Be4) he felt was too 'human'; IBM denied any in-game intervention, stating the only changes to the program were made between games as the rules allowed, and later published Deep Blue's log files online.
trivia.source: Chess.com: 'Did IBM Cheat Kasparov?'; Wikipedia: Deep Blue versus Garry Kasparov

trivia.fact: IBM declined Kasparov's request for a rematch and retired Deep Blue after the 1997 match; parts of the machine are now preserved and displayed at the Smithsonian Institution and the Computer History Museum.
trivia.source: Chess.com forums: 'Why was Deep Blue disassembled by IBM'; IBM history site

trivia.fact: In October 2002, world champion Vladimir Kramnik played an eight-game match ('Brains in Bahrain') against Deep Fritz 7 in Manama, Bahrain, which ended in a 4-4 tie (two wins each, four draws).
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Brains in Bahrain; ChessBase: '20 years ago: Brains in Bahrain'

trivia.fact: In January-February 2003, Garry Kasparov played a six-game match in New York against Deep Junior (developed by Amir Ban and Shay Bushinsky), which ended 3-3.
trivia.source: Chessprogramming wiki: Kasparov versus Deep Junior 2003; ChessBase

trivia.fact: In November 2003, Garry Kasparov played a four-game match against X3D Fritz (viewed through 3D glasses), which ended tied 2-2, with one win apiece and two draws.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: X3D Fritz; Chessprogramming wiki: Kasparov versus X3D Fritz 2003

trivia.fact: In the November-December 2006 match in Bonn, Germany, Deep Fritz defeated reigning world champion Vladimir Kramnik 4-2, the last major human-vs-top-engine match before engines pulled decisively ahead of the best humans.
trivia.source: ChessBase: 'Kramnik vs Deep Fritz: Computer wins match by 4:2'

trivia.fact: The Stockfish chess engine began as a fork of Tord Romstad's open-source Glaurung engine; Marco Costalba released the first version, Stockfish 1.0, in November 2008. Its name reflects that it was 'produced in Norway [Romstad] and cooked in Italy [Costalba].'

Stockfish is released under the GNU General Public License (GPL v3) and has been developed since 2013 using the crowdsourced distributed-testing framework 'Fishtest,' created by Gary Linscott, in which volunteers donate CPU time to statistically validate proposed code changes; Stockfish reportedly gained about 120 Elo points in the 12 months after Fishtest's introduction.

Vasik Rajlich released the first public beta of his engine Rybka (Czech/Slavic for 'little fish') on December 5, 2005; Rybka went on to win the World Computer Chess Championship four consecutive times, 2007-2010.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Rybka; Bill Wall's Rybka article

trivia.fact: On June 28, 2011, the International Computer Games Association (ICGA) ruled that Vasik Rajlich's Rybka had plagiarized code from the Crafty and Fruit engines, stripped Rybka of its 2006-2010 World Computer Chess Championship titles, ordered return of prize money and trophies, and banned Rajlich for life from ICGA-sanctioned events.
trivia.source: Chess.com: 'Rybka disqualified and banned from World Computer Chess Championships'

trivia.fact: Robert Houdart released the first version of his engine Houdini for free download in May 2010; by July 2010, Houdini 1.03a already rated about 3116 Elo on the CCRL 40/4 list, and within months it displaced Rybka as the world's top-rated engine.
trivia.source: Chessprogramming wiki: Robert Houdart; ChessBase: '10 years Houdini'

trivia.fact: Houdini won the first two seasons of the Top Chess Engine Championship (TCEC), in 2010 and 2011, ahead of Rybka and other leading engines of the time.

The Komodo chess engine began in 2007 as a collaboration between programmer Don Dailey and grandmaster Larry Kaufman, evolving out of Dailey's earlier engine Doch; Komodo was later acquired by Chess.com in 2018.
trivia.source: ChessBase: 'Komodo: Birth of a chess engine'; Wikipedia: Komodo (chess)

trivia.fact: Don Dailey announced in October 2013, at the release of Komodo 6, that he had been diagnosed with acute leukemia and would step back from development; programmer Mark Lefler joined the Komodo team days later to continue the project. Dailey died in November 2013.

The Top Chess Engine Championship (TCEC) was launched in 2010 by Norwegian programmer Martin Thoresen as the 'Thoresen Chess Engines Competition'; after a hiatus it relaunched in 2013 and has been organized by Chessdom since Season 7.
Chess.com launched its own engine event, the Computer Chess Championship (originally CCCC), in November 2017 with ten of the strongest engines competing for $2,500 in prize money.
trivia.source: Chess.com: 'The First Computer Chess Championship in the USA'

trivia.fact: DeepMind posted its AlphaZero preprint to arXiv on December 5, 2017 (arXiv:1712.01815), reporting that a single algorithm using self-play reinforcement learning and Monte Carlo tree search had reached superhuman level in chess, shogi, and Go within 24 hours of self-training, defeating Stockfish, the shogi engine Elmo, and a 3-day version of AlphaGo Zero.
trivia.source: arXiv:1712.01815; DeepMind blog 'AlphaZero: Shedding new light on chess, shogi, and Go'

trivia.fact: In its first published 100-game match (December 2017 preprint) against Stockfish 8, AlphaZero scored 28 wins, 0 losses, and 72 draws under a fixed one-minute-per-move time control.
trivia.source: Chess.com: 'Google's AlphaZero Destroys Stockfish In 100-Game Match'; chessgames.com AlphaZero-Stockfish 2017 event page

trivia.fact: The peer-reviewed version of the AlphaZero research, 'A general reinforcement learning algorithm that masters chess, shogi and Go through self-play,' was published in the journal Science on December 7, 2018 (Silver et al., Science 362(6419):1140-1144), using improved test conditions (Stockfish given an opening book and access to Syzygy tablebases) after criticism of the original 2017 match setup.
trivia.source: Science 362(6419):1140-1144; ChessBase 'The full AlphaZero paper is published at long last'

trivia.fact: In the revised 2018 Science-paper match, a 1,000-game contest between AlphaZero and Stockfish 8 ended 155 wins, 6 losses, and 839 draws in AlphaZero's favor.
trivia.source: Chess.com: 'AlphaZero Crushes Stockfish In New 1,000-Game Match'

trivia.fact: According to DeepMind, AlphaZero's chess-specific training required about 9 hours of self-play (compared with about 12 hours for shogi and roughly 13 days for Go) before reaching the reported superhuman benchmark.
trivia.source: DeepMind blog: 'AlphaZero: Shedding new light on chess, shogi, and Go'

trivia.fact: Leela Chess Zero (Lc0), an open-source engine inspired by DeepMind's AlphaZero approach and adapted from the Leela Zero Go project, was launched by Gary Linscott (a former Stockfish contributor) in January 2018 and trains its neural network via distributed, crowdsourced self-play games contributed by volunteers.
trivia.source: Chess.com: 'Leela Chess Zero: A History'; Wikipedia: Leela Chess Zero

trivia.fact: Leela Chess Zero made its TCEC debut in Division 4 of Season 12 in April 2018 as the first neural-network engine to compete in TCEC, initially losing almost every game before rapidly improving.
trivia.source: CentAUR: 'TCEC12: the 12th Top Chess Engine Championship'

trivia.fact: In February 2019, Leela Chess Zero won the TCEC Cup by defeating Houdini in the final, becoming the first neural-network engine to win a major TCEC title.
trivia.source: Chessdom: 'First major title for a Neural Network in chess: LC0 wins TCEC Cup'

trivia.fact: In May 2019, Leela Chess Zero won the TCEC Season 15 Superfinal against Stockfish 53.5-46.5 (14 wins, 7 losses, 79 draws) -- the first time a neural-network engine won a TCEC Superfinal.

NNUE (Efficiently Updatable Neural Network) evaluation, invented by Yu Nasu in 2018 for the shogi engine YaneuraOu, was ported into Stockfish and merged into the Stockfish source repository on August 6, 2020, producing an estimated 80-100 Elo jump in engine-testing strength -- the first time a top classical chess engine successfully paired a CPU-efficient neural network with traditional alpha-beta search.
trivia.source: Stockfish blog: 'Introducing NNUE Evaluation'; Chessprogramming wiki: Stockfish NNUE

trivia.fact: Following Stockfish's NNUE adoption in 2020, other top engines including Komodo (rebranded 'Dragon by Komodo Chess'), Ethereal, Igel, and Scorpio also added NNUE-based evaluation within the following year.
trivia.source: dev.to: 'Why Stockfish is So Good'; Chess.com: 'Evolution of a Chess Fish: What is NNUE, anyway?'

trivia.fact: University at Buffalo computer science professor Kenneth Regan developed the primary statistical cheating-detection methodology used by FIDE, which computes a player's 'Intrinsic Performance Rating' (IPR) from move-by-move engine agreement and flags suspicious deviation from a player's official rating using a z-score, with FIDE's suspicion threshold set at a z-score of about 4.5.
trivia.source: TIME: '"Chess Detective" Probes Magnus Carlsen, Hans Niemann Case'; ChessBase: 'Prof. Regan's statistical system'

trivia.fact: FIDE has paid Kenneth Regan to monitor tournaments since 2020, and his proprietary engine-based cheat-detection software has by his account analyzed more than a million games.
trivia.source: TIME: '"Chess Detective" Probes Magnus Carlsen, Hans Niemann Case'

trivia.fact: Deep Blue's predecessor Deep Thought used custom VLSI chess-search chips and could evaluate up to about 700,000 chess positions per second, several hundred times slower than the 480-chip Deep Blue system that beat Kasparov in 1997.

IBM's Deep Blue project traced its lineage through a sequence of machines built by Feng-hsiung Hsu -- ChipTest, then Deep Thought, then Deep Blue -- spanning roughly a decade of hardware-accelerated chess search research from the mid-1980s to 1997.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Feng-hsiung Hsu; Wikipedia: Deep Blue (chess computer)

trivia.fact: FIDE (the International Chess Federation) was founded on 20 July 1924 in Paris, at the Paris town hall of the 9th Arrondissement, on the closing day of the first (unofficial) Chess Olympiad held alongside the 1924 Summer Olympics.

FIDE's founding Proclamation Act was signed by fifteen delegates representing countries including Argentina, Belgium, Britain, France, Hungary, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Canada, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Finland, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia.
trivia.source: FIDE official history (museum.fide.com/fide-history); Chess.com, "How was FIDE created?"

trivia.fact: FIDE's motto, "Gens Una Sumus" (Latin for "We Are One Family"), traces to a 1945 message from FIDE's first president Alexander Rueb about chess as a force for international understanding, and was first used in print by FIDE in 1952.
trivia.source: Chess.com, "Gens Una Sumus"; Edward Winter, "The History of FIDE" (chesshistory.com)

trivia.fact: Alexander Rueb of the Netherlands served as FIDE's first president, beginning at its founding in 1924.
The first FIDE-organized official Chess Olympiad took place in London from 18 to 30 July 1927, at Westminster Central Hall, with 16 teams (70 players) competing; Hungary won the gold medal.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: 1st Chess Olympiad; OlimpBase, 1st Chess Olympiad, London 1927

trivia.fact: The trophy awarded to the winning team in the Chess Olympiad's open section, the Hamilton-Russell Cup, was donated by English chess patron Sir Frederick Hamilton-Russell as a prize for the first Olympiad in London, 1927.
Since 1950, the Chess Olympiad has been held every two years on a regular biennial schedule; before World War II it took place only occasionally and at irregular intervals.

The Soviet Union won 18 gold medals in the open Chess Olympiad between 1952 and 1990, the most of any nation in the event's history, placing first in every edition it entered during that span except 1978 (it boycotted 1976).
trivia.source: Chess.com, "The Chess Olympiad: By The Numbers"; House of Staunton, "Guide to the Chess Olympiad"

trivia.fact: The first Women's Chess Olympiad was held in Emmen, Netherlands, in 1957, hosted by the Royal Dutch Chess Federation, with 22 nations competing in a two-player-per-team format.
The Staunton chess set design was registered as an "Ornamental Design for a set of Chess-Men" at the British Patent Office on 1 March 1849, under the name of English journalist Nathaniel Cooke.

The Staunton set was first manufactured and sold by the firm John Jaques of London starting in 1849, and the pattern was named after English chess master Howard Staunton, who endorsed it though he did not design it.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Staunton chess set; Smithsonian Magazine, "How the Chess Set Got Its Look and Feel"

trivia.fact: The first 500 Staunton chess sets sold by Jaques of London were individually numbered and hand-signed by Howard Staunton himself.

The knight piece in the Staunton chess set design is modeled on the carved horse head from the chariot of the moon goddess Selene, part of the Parthenon's east pediment sculptures (the Elgin Marbles) held in the British Museum.

The first mechanical chess clock, consisting of two spring-driven clocks balanced on a seesaw beam, was built in 1883 by Thomas Bright Wilson of Manchester, England, with input from chess master Joseph Henry Blackburne.
trivia.source: History of Chess Clocks (innovationcorridor.net); billwall.phpwebhosting.com, "Chess Clocks"

trivia.fact: Chess clocks were used in a tournament for the first time at London 1883, with a time control of 15 moves in two hours; the first patent for a chess clock followed in 1884, issued to Amandus Schierwater of Liverpool.
The first digital chess clock was built in 1973 by Bruce Cheney, a Cornell University electrical-engineering student, as an undergraduate course project.
trivia.source: Chess.com, "Evolution of Chess Clocks and Increment"

trivia.fact: The first commercially available digital chess clock, the Micromate-80, was created in 1975 by Joseph Meshi and Jeffrey R. Ponsor.
trivia.source: Chess.com, "Evolution of Chess Clocks and Increment"

trivia.fact: In 1988, former World Champion Bobby Fischer patented a digital chess clock design that introduced the "Fischer increment," adding a fixed amount of time to a player's clock after each move.
trivia.source: Chess.com, "Evolution of Chess Clocks and Increment"

trivia.fact: The "Bronstein delay" time-control method, named after Soviet grandmaster David Bronstein, adds back only as much time as a player actually used on a move, up to a fixed cap, rather than always adding the full increment.
trivia.source: Chess.com, "Evolution of Chess Clocks and Increment"

trivia.fact: The Elo chess rating system was created by Arpad Elo, a Hungarian-American physics professor at Marquette University in Milwaukee, who chaired a USCF committee tasked in 1959 with evaluating rating systems.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Arpad Elo; Wikipedia: Elo rating system

trivia.fact: The United States Chess Federation adopted the Elo rating system in 1960, at its meeting in Saint Louis, replacing the previously used Harkness rating system.
trivia.source: House of Staunton, "How The Elo Chess Rating System Works"; Wikipedia: Elo rating system

trivia.fact: FIDE formally adopted the Elo rating system for international chess ratings in 1970.
Arpad Elo's book "The Rating of Chessplayers, Past and Present," the first publicly available text describing his rating system in full, was published in 1978.
trivia.source: FIDE, "Anniversary of Arpad Elo"; Wikipedia: Arpad Elo

trivia.fact: FIDE created the titles Grandmaster (GM), International Master (IM), and Woman International Master in 1950, formalizing an initial list of 27 Grandmasters at its Congress in Copenhagen that July.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Grandmaster (chess); mieses.info, "The First FIDE Grandmasters 1950"

trivia.fact: Chess master Jacques Mieses, at age 85, was the oldest player among FIDE's inaugural group of 27 Grandmasters named in 1950.

Because FIDE does not award chess titles posthumously, former World Champions Wilhelm Steinitz, Emanuel Lasker, José Raúl Capablanca, and Alexander Alekhine — all deceased before 1950 — never held the official FIDE Grandmaster title.
FIDE did not introduce formal, norm-based requirements for earning the Grandmaster title until 1957; before that, titles were awarded by committee resolution without written criteria.

An early forerunner of algebraic chess notation was published by Philipp Stamma, a chess player born in Aleppo, in his 1737 book "Essai sur le Jeu des Echecs" (English edition, 1745: "The Noble Game of Chess"), using files a-h and ranks 1-8.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: Algebraic notation (chess); Chess.com, "The Creator of Algebraic Chess Notation"

trivia.fact: Stamma's original notation differed from modern algebraic notation in using the letter "P" for pawn moves and a capital letter (A-H) for a piece's originating file, rather than the piece's initial letter.

Descriptive notation, not algebraic, remained the standard in English-language chess publications until FIDE stopped officially recognizing it in 1981, after which algebraic notation became the sole internationally required system.
The first postage stamp with a chess theme was issued by Bulgaria on 29 September 1947, part of a set commemorating the 1947 Balkan Games in Sofia, depicting a knight chess piece.
trivia.source: billwall.phpwebhosting.com, "History of stamps and chess"; Edward Winter, "Chess and Postage Stamps"

trivia.fact: The first postage stamp to depict an actual chess player was issued by Cuba on 1 November 1951, part of a set marking the 30th anniversary of José Raúl Capablanca's 1921 World Championship win over Emanuel Lasker.
Hungary issued three chess-themed postage stamps on 9 April 1950 to commemorate the first Candidates Tournament, held in Budapest from April 9 to May 16, 1950.

The World Chess Hall of Fame was founded in 1986 by Steven Doyle, then president of the U.S. Chess Federation, and opened to the public in 1988 in the basement of the USCF's headquarters in New Windsor, New York.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: World Chess Hall of Fame

trivia.fact: The World Chess Hall of Fame relocated to Saint Louis, Missouri, on September 9, 2011, in a building renovated with funding from philanthropist Rex Sinquefield, located across the street from the Sinquefield-founded Saint Louis Chess Club.
trivia.source: Wikipedia: World Chess Hall of Fame

trivia.fact: Fischer Random Chess (later known as Chess960) was formally introduced to the public by Bobby Fischer on 19 June 1996 in Buenos Aires, Argentina, under the name "Fischerandom Chess."

Chess960 is named for the 960 possible distinct starting arrangements of the back-rank pieces (with bishops on opposite-colored squares and the king between the rooks), a figure Fischer had mathematicians compute while he was in Budapest.

The chess variant Kriegspiel, in which each player cannot see the opponent's pieces and a neutral umpire adjudicates move legality, was invented in 1899 by Henry Michael Temple, adapting the concept from an 1812 Prussian military training wargame called Kriegsspiel devised by Georg von Reiswitz.

Xiangqi (Chinese chess) and Shogi (Japanese chess) both trace to a common ancestor, the Indian game chaturanga (roughly 3rd-6th century CE), the same game that spread west through Persia to become Western chess.
trivia.source: ancientgames.org, "Chess vs Shogi vs Xiangqi: Three Paths from Chaturanga"

trivia.fact: The earliest documentary evidence of shogi in Japan appears in the Shin Sarugakuki, a literary work by Fujiwara no Akihira written around 1058-1064 CE.
The sport of chess boxing was inspired by French comic-book artist Enki Bilal's 1992 graphic novel "Froid Équateur," which depicted a fictional chess-boxing world championship.

Dutch performance artist Iepe Rubingh turned the comic-book concept into a real competitive sport, staging the first official chess boxing match in Berlin in 2003, which he won to become the first World Chess Boxing Champion.

Walter Tevis's 1983 novel "The Queen's Gambit" got its title from a suggestion by chess master Bruce Pandolfini, who consulted on the book's chess content and proposed naming it after the chess opening of the same name.
Following the October 2020 release of Netflix's "The Queen's Gambit" miniseries starring Anya Taylor-Joy, U.S. game maker Goliath Games reported chess set sales increasing by more than 1,000 percent.

"Searching for Bobby Fischer" (1993), directed by Steven Zaillian, dramatizes the real early chess career of prodigy Josh Waitzkin and is based on the memoir of the same name by his father, Fred Waitzkin.

Austrian writer Stefan Zweig's novella "Schachnovelle" (published in English as "The Royal Game" or "Chess Story") was the last work of fiction he completed, written in exile in Brazil in 1941 and published in 1942, the year of his death.

Lewis Carroll structured his 1871 novel "Through the Looking-Glass" around a chess game, with protagonist Alice cast as a white pawn who journeys across the board and is crowned a queen in the final chapters; Carroll prefaced the book with an actual chess-move diagram.
Satyajit Ray's 1977 film "Shatranj Ke Khilari" ("The Chess Players"), based on a short story by Munshi Premchand and set in 1856 Awadh, was Ray's only full-length feature film made in Hindi.

"Pawn Sacrifice" (2014), directed by Edward Zwick and starring Tobey Maguire as Bobby Fischer and Liev Schreiber as Boris Spassky, dramatizes the 1972 World Chess Championship match in Reykjavik, Iceland.

The United States Chess Federation was formed in 1939 through the merger of two older organizations, the American Chess Federation and the National Chess Federation, and took over the NCF's management of the U.S. Championship and its FIDE affiliation.

Bughouse chess, a team variant played on two boards where captured pieces are handed to a partner to "drop" onto their own board, emerged organically among players in the United States and Europe in the early 1960s with no single identifiable inventor.
trivia.source: the-pechko-perspective.com, "Bughouse Chess: The Wild History of Chess's Most Exciting Variant"
